title: The Acute Effects of 60 Gramms of Glucose During Resistance Training at 80% of One-Repetition Maximum on Performance, Fatigue, Energy Metabolism and Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness: A Randomized Controlled Crossover Study
summary: In endurance sports, carbohydrates consumed during exercise are known to help maintain performance for longer. Whether this also applies to realistic resistance training has been studied only to a limited extent. In this study we compare how resistance training with and without a carbohydrate drink affects performance, fatigue, well-being and muscle soreness. Adults aged 18 to 40 years with resistance training experience complete two training sessions of 60 to 90 minutes with exercises for the legs, back and chest. In one session they drink a beverage containing carbohydrates and in the other a beverage without carbohydrates. The order is determined by chance. Before and after training, blood glucose and lactate are measured from a drop of blood taken from the earlobe, and strength and jump tests are performed. On the two days after training, participants are asked about muscle soreness.
conditions: No diseases are investigated. The study is conducted in healthy, resistance-trained adults. It examines acute physiological and subjective responses to resistance exercise (muscular fatigue, performance, metabolic parameters and muscle soreness in the sense of delayed onset muscle soreness) depending on carbohydrate intake.

interventions.name: Carbohydrate drink. Participants complete a resistance training session of 60 to 90 minutes (leg press, machine knee extension and squat, cable lat pulldown, free-weight bench press, 3 sets each at 80% of one-repetition maximum with an individual repetition number standardized across conditions). Placebo. Identical resistance training session as in group 1. During the session participants drink 500 ml of water containing 0.5 g citric acid and 0.5 g sodium chloride without carbohydrate.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Previous experience in resistance training
Voluntary participation and written informed consent
Full legal capacity and understanding of the nature, scope, significance and consequences of the study
Exclusion criteria:
Acute injuries or severe diseases that affect quality of life or physical performance capacity, in particular cardiovascular, pulmonary or renal dysfunction, neurological or psychiatric disorders, advanced degenerative diseases of the musculoskeletal system, and incompletely healed sports injuries
